sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Nuada** (*nuada*) ​— War, ‌King of ‌Tuatha · ​Cloud-maker, hunter ​— belongs ​to the ​Celtic tradition, ​where it ‌is catalogued ​under the ​domain "War, ‌King of ​Tuatha". The ‌name means ​"Cloud-maker, hunter"[^1].

‌Nuada Airgetlám ​is the ​**first king of ​the Tuatha ​Dé Danann ​in Ireland** ‌— the ​ruler who ‌lost his ​arm at ‌the First ​Battle of ‌Mag Tuired, ​lost his ‌throne to ​the law ​that a ‌blemished man ‌cannot be ‌king, and won ​both back ​through the ‌physicians' craft: ​first the ​silver arm ‌that named ​him, then ​the living ‌arm that ​restored him. ‌His sword ​from Findias ​was one ​of the ​Four Treasures ‌of his ‌people, and ​he died at ‌the Second ​Battle of ​Mag Tuired ‌at the ‌hands of ‌Balor of ‌the Evil ​Eye.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores the ​name as ​**Nuada** and ​serves its ‌temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/nuada/). ​The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ‌— a description ​computed from ​the displayed ​form itself. ‌The plain ​ASCII form ‌*nuada* survives ​as a ‌modern convenience ​imposed by ‌the early ‌domain-name system; ​the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous ‌written attestation ‌survives ​for ​this ​name; ​**Nuada** is ​a ‌scholarly ​transliteration ​of the ‌reconstructed ​spoken ‌form. ​Etymologically the ‌name ​means ​"Cloud-maker, ​hunter"[^1].

​The ASCII ​form ‌*nuada* ​survives ‌only because ​the ‌early ​domain-name ‌system ​could not ‌carry ​diacritics; ​it ‌is a ‌technological ‌compromise, ​not ​an ancient ‌spelling. ​The ​Unicode ‌restoration ​**Nuada** recovers ​the ‌full ​diacritic ‌detail of ​the ​scholarly ​transliteration ​directly ‌in the ‌address ​bar. ‌The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ‌— ‌a ‌description computed ‌from ​the ‌displayed ​form ​itself.

The ​letter-by-letter ‌transformation ​runs:

- ​**n** → ​**N** ‌— ​Same, ​capitalized
- ​**u** → ‌**u** ​— ‌Same
- ​**a** → ‌**a** ​— ‌Same
- ‌**d** → ​**d** ​— ​Same
- ​**a** ‌→ **a** ‌— ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of the ‌name is **/ˈnuː.að.u/** ‌— Old Irish ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- ​**N-** — Broad ​alveolar nasal [n̪ˠ], ​the plain 'n' ​of Old Irish ‌initial position, unlenited.
- ​**-uːa-** — Long ​close back [uː] ‌gliding into open ​[a]; the two vowels ‌of Nuadu fall ​across a syllable ‌boundary.
- **-ð-** — ​Lenited d, the ​voiced dental fricative ​[ð] — the ​soft 'th' of ​'this', which medieval ‌Irish scribes wrote simply ​as d.
- **-u** ‌— Short back ​[u], the final ‌vowel of the ​Old Irish nominative ‌form Nuadu.

For ​the modern speaker, ‌the closest approximation ​is: 'NOO-ah-oo' — stress ​the first syllable, ‌hold the 'oo' ‌long, soften the ‌middle d toward ​the 'th' of ​'breathe', and finish ‌on a short ​'oo'. Modern English ​speakers usually say 'NOO-uh-duh'.

‌Kindred and historical ​forms of the ​name:

- **Old Irish** ‌— Nuadu (later ​Nuada), byname Airgetlám, ‌'Silver-hand'
- **Middle Welsh** ​— Nudd, and ​Lludd Llaw Eraint, 'Lludd ​of the Silver ​Hand', king of ‌Britain in Lludd ‌a Llefelys
- **Gaulish** ​— Nodens (also ‌Nodons, Nudens), the ​god of the ​temple at Lydney ‌Park in Gloucestershire
- **Modern ‌Irish** — Nuadha, ‌the living spelling ‌of the name

​Nuada is a ‌plain restoration by ​the mechanical rule: ​the attested Old ​Irish form carries ‌no diacritic and no ​distinctive letter, so ​plain ASCII loses ​nothing. The etymology ‌is honestly uncertain: ​one proposal reads ​the name as ​'cloud-maker', from a ‌root behind Welsh ​nudd 'mist'; another, argued ‌by Tolkien for ​the Gaulish Nodens, ‌connects it to ​a root meaning ‌'to catch, acquire' ‌— a fisher ​or hunter — ​which would suit ​the sea-and-hounds imagery of ​the Lydney temple. ‌Neither is settled, ‌and the temple ​says so.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous writing ‌system is ‌securely ​attested for ​individual ​celtic names. ​The form ​shown ‌is a ​modern ​scholarly transliteration.[^1]

‌The form ​**Nuada** ‌is therefore ​a ‌scholarly transliteration ​rather than ​an ​attested ancient ​spelling; ​it encodes ‌the reconstructed ​sound ‌of the ​name ‌for modern ​use, and ‌no ​mark in ‌it ​is decorative.

​The attested ‌Old ‌Irish form ‌is ​**Nuadu** (later ​**Nuada**), written ‌by ​medieval Irish ​scribes ‌in the ​Insular Latin ​bookhand ‌of the ​great ‌vellum codices; ​in the ​Ogham ​letter-row the ​name ‌would have ‌been notched ​ᚅᚒᚐᚇᚐ ‌(N-U-A-D-A), though ​no ​Ogham stone ‌yet found ‌carries ‌it. Because ‌the ​name is ‌already plain ​ASCII, ​its domain ​was ‌registered decades ​ago in ​the ​ordinary way: ‌**nuada.com ​is held ​by a ​third ‌party outside ​the ‌PuniCodex collection ​and is ‌watched ​for release** ‌— ‌no form ​of the ​name ​is currently ​owned, ‌and this ‌temple claims ​none.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Nuada Airgetlám ​is the ‌**first king ‌of the ​Tuatha Dé ​Danann in ​Ireland** — the ​ruler who ​lost his ‌arm at ​the First ​Battle of ‌Mag Tuired, lost ​his throne ‌to the ​law that ‌a blemished ​man cannot ​be king, and ​won both ​back through ​the physicians' ‌craft: first ​the silver arm ‌that named ​him, then ‌the living ​arm that ‌restored him. ​His sword from ‌Findias was ​one of ​the Four ‌Treasures of ‌his people, ‌and he died ​at the ​Second Battle ‌of Mag ​Tuired at ​the hands ‌of Balor of ​the Evil ​Eye.[^1]

### The ‌Silver Hand

​Dian Cécht's ‌silver arm, ​made with Credne ​the brazier, ​moved in ​every joint ‌— and ‌gave the ​king his name, ‌Airgetlám.

### The ​Sword from ​Findias

One ‌of the ‌Four Treasures ‌of the Tuatha ‌Dé Danann; ​once it ‌was drawn ​from its ​sheath, no ​one escaped it.

### ‌Mag Tuired

​The plain ​of the ​two battles: ‌against the Fir ​Bolg, where ​the arm ​was lost; ‌against the ​Fomorians, where ‌the king fell.

### ​The Unblemished ‌Throne

Irish ​kingship law ‌held that ‌no man ​with a blemish ​could rule; ​Nuada's wound ​cost him ‌Tara, and ‌his healing ​restored him.

sources.citation: Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Mag Tuired), ed. and trans. Elizabeth A. Gray, Irish Texts Society 52 (1982) — Lugh's coming to Tara and Nuada's death at Balor's hand.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography associated ‌with ‌Nuada ​concentrates in ​a ​small ​set of ​recurring ‌attributes, ​each a ​compressed ‌statement about ​the ‌name:[^1]

- ​**The silver ‌arm** ​— ​Wholeness made ​by ​craft ​when nature ‌failed ​— the ‌prosthesis ​that ‌kept a ​king ‌king ​in all ‌but ​law
- ​**The sword ‌of ‌Nuada** — ‌The ​irresistible ​weapon from ‌the ​city ​Findias, one ‌of ​the ​Four Treasures ‌brought ​to Ireland
- ‌**Tara ​(Temair)** ​— The ​seat ​of ‌the kingship ‌of ​Ireland, ‌which a ​blemished ​man could ‌not ‌lawfully ‌hold
- **The ‌physician's ​craft** ‌— Dian ​Cécht's ​silver-work ​and Miach's ‌flesh-work ​— healing ​as ​the ‌instrument of ​sovereignty
- ​**Dog ​and fisherman ‌(as ​Nodens)** ‌— The ​hound ‌figurines and ​sea ‌imagery ‌of the ​Lydney ​Park ​temple, where ​his ‌Gaulish ‌cognate was ​worshipped

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Nuada's story is the ​Irish tradition's great parable of kingship and ‌the body: a ruler can be unmade by ‌a single wound and remade by healing, ​and the law watches both. The record ​runs from the Lebor Gabála Érenn through the ​two battles of Mag Tuired, and his ​Welsh and Gaulish cognates carry the same ​silver-handed name across the Celtic world.[^1]

### The First ‌Battle of Mag Tuired (Lebor Gabála Érenn)

​When the Tuatha Dé Danann came to ​Ireland, Nuada had been their king for seven ‌years. They demanded the country from the ​Fir Bolg, and the two peoples met ‌at Mag Tuired in Connacht. In the ​battle Nuada fought Sreng, champion of the Fir ‌Bolg, and Sreng struck off his right ​arm at the shoulder — yet the ​Tuatha Dé Danann won the field, and the ​Fir Bolg king Eochaid mac Eirc was ​driven to his death. The victors then ​offered the defeated a quarter of Ireland, and ‌the Fir Bolg chose Connacht, which their ​descendants held. The victory that made the ‌Tuatha Dé Danann masters of Ireland thus cost ​their king the wholeness the kingship required: ‌one champion's sword-stroke bought a kingdom and ​unmade its king in the same afternoon.[^2]

### ‌The Silver Hand and the Hand of Flesh ​(Lebor Gabála Érenn)

Because a blemished man ‌could not hold the kingship, Nuada yielded ​the throne to Bres. The physician Dian Cécht, ​with Credne the brazier, made him a ‌full arm of silver that moved in ‌every joint — whence his byname Airgetlám, Silver-hand. ‌But Dian Cécht's own son Miach went ​further: he set the severed arm to ​the stump and healed it 'joint to joint ‌and vein to vein' in thrice nine ​days. Jealous that the son had outdone ​the father, Dian Cécht struck Miach dead; ‌from the young healer's grave grew three hundred ​and sixty-five herbs, which his sister Airmed ​sorted by their virtues — and which ‌Dian Cécht scattered, so that their full knowledge ​died with him. Healing, in this cycle, ‌is never free of the wound of ​envy.

### Bres, the Satire, and the Restoration (Lebor ​Gabála · Cath Maige Tuired)

Bres mac ​Elatha, half Fomorian by blood, ruled badly: ​the warriors of Ireland were set to ‌menial labour, hospitality failed, and the poet Cairbre ‌mac Étaíne composed against him what the ​tradition calls the first satire ever made ‌in Ireland — and Bres's face broke out ​in blotches. Shamed and deposed, Bres fled ​to his Fomorian kin and came back ‌at the head of the host that forced ‌the Second Battle. The same law that ‌had unseated Nuada now unseated Bres, for ‌a blemished king could not stand; and with ​his arm made whole by Miach, Nuada ‌took back the kingship and held it ​until the war came. The symmetry is ​exact: one king falls by the body's wound, ​the other by the wound of the ‌word, and the same unforgiving law of ​wholeness judges them both.

### The Second Battle and ​the King's Death (Cath Maige Tuired)

At ​Tara, on the eve of the war, ‌a stranger came to Nuada's hall claiming every ​skill at once — harpist, warrior, smith, ​poet, healer — and Nuada, testing Lugh ​and finding him unmatched, gave the young god ‌his own seat, the champion's seat, to ​lead the counsel of war. The Second ‌Battle of Mag Tuired was fought against ​the Fomorians, and there Nuada Airgetlám and Macha ‌his wife fell together at the hands ​of Balor of the Evil Eye. Balor's ‌own death followed within the hour, Lugh's sling-stone ‌through the destroying eye, and with the ​two kings' deaths the war ended and ​the tribute was lifted forever. The first king ​of the Tuatha Dé Danann in Ireland ​died in the victory that secured his ‌people's rule; the sword of Findias passed into ‌memory as the measure of a weapon ​that cannot be withstood.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Nuada ​belongs to ‌one of ‌the clearest ​pan-Celtic name ​families. In ​Welsh he ​is ​**Nudd** and, ‌in full ​form, **Lludd ​Llaw Eraint** ‌— 'Lludd ​of the ‌Silver Hand' ​— ‌the king ​of Britain ​in *Lludd ​a Llefelys*, ​whose byname ​renders Airgetlám ‌word ​for word ‌(llaw 'hand', ​eraint 'silver'). ‌In Gaulish ​he is ‌**Nodens** (also ​Nodons, ‌Nudens), worshipped ​at the ​great temple ‌at Lydney ‌Park in ‌Gloucestershire, where ​Roman dedicants ​equated ‌him with ​Mars and ​where the ‌imagery — ​hounds, fishermen, ​the sea ‌— ​suggests a ‌healer and ​hunter as ​much as ​a warrior. ​The Romano-British ‌curse ‌tablet of ​Silvianus, asking ‌'Lord Nodens' ​to deny ​health to ‌the thief ‌of his ‌ring, ‌shows the ​god working ‌as an ​enforcer of ​justice. Scholars ​(Mac Cana, ‌Koch) ​reconstruct a ​Common Celtic ​*Noudont- or ‌*Noudo- behind ​all three, ​though the ​root's ‌meaning — ​'cloud-maker' or ‌'catcher, fisher' ​— remains ‌genuinely debated.[^1]

​Within the ‌Celtic tradition, ‌closely ​related names ​in the ​corpus include ​[[aengus|Aengus]], [[annwn|Annwn]], ‌[[arawn|Arawn]], [[badb|Badb]], ‌[[balor|Balor]], and ​[[bedwyr|Bedwyr]].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Nuada's ​afterlife runs ‌through ‌scholarship into ​fantasy. When ​R. ​E. M. ​and ​T. V. ‌Wheeler published ​their ​excavation of ‌the ​Nodens temple ‌at Lydney ​Park ‌in 1932, ​the ​young philologist ​J. R. ​R. ​Tolkien contributed ‌the ​appendix 'The ‌Name ​Nodens', tracing ‌the god's ​name ‌to a ​root ‌of catching ​and acquiring ​— ‌a fragment ‌of ‌Tolkien's scholarly ​life that ​fans ‌of his ​fiction ​still chase. ‌In modern ​Irish ​the name ‌survives ​as Nuadha, ‌and ​Maynooth University's ​old arms ​carried ​Nuada's sword. ‌In ‌popular culture ​the silver-handed ‌king ​rides again ​as ‌Prince Nuada ‌Silverlance in ‌*Hellboy ‌II: The ​Golden ‌Army* (2008), ​and the ​motif ​of the ‌magical ​prosthetic hand ​— ​from *A ‌Song of ​Ice ​and Fire* ​to ‌Japanese fantasy ​— descends, ‌knowingly ​or not, ‌from ​Airgetlám. Modern ‌Celtic pagans ‌honour ​Nuada as ​a ​god of ​rightful rule, ‌healing, ‌and sovereignty ​restored.[^1]

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: Nuada is ​textual in ‌Ireland — ‌no inscription ​names him ​there — ​but his ​Gaulish cognate ​has one ‌of the ​best-excavated cult ​sites in Roman ‌Britain. At ​Lydney Park, ‌Gloucestershire, overlooking ​the Severn ‌estuary, a ​temple complex ​of the ​late third ​and fourth ​centuries CE ‌was dedicated to ​Nodens: the ‌Wheelers' excavations ​(1928–29, published ‌1932 with ​Tolkien's philological ‌appendix) uncovered ​mosaic floors, ‌inscribed slabs ​reading DEVO ​NODENTI and ‌D M NODONTI ‌('to the ‌god Mars ​Nodens'), bronze ​dog figurines, ‌a fisherman ​plaque, and ​pins and ‌bracelets left ​as votives ​— the ‌material of a ​healing-and-hunting cult. ‌The famous ​curse tablet ​of Silvianus, ​asking Nodens ​to withhold ‌health from ‌whoever stole ​his ring ‌until it ​was returned 'to ​the temple ‌of Nodens', ‌was found ‌on the ‌site; a ​gold ring ‌inscribed SENICIANE ​VIVAS IN ​DEO, plausibly ​the very ‌ring, surfaced at ​Silchester. On ​the Irish ​side, the ‌texts are ​the evidence: ​the Second ​Battle of ‌Mag Tuired ​survives in ‌the sixteenth-century ​British Library Harley ‌MS 5280, ​the First ‌Battle in ‌a single ​late vellum ​copy edited ​by Fraser, ​and the ‌Lebor Gabála ‌in its ​medieval recensions.[^1]

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Nuada ​is the ‌king of ‌the necessary ​surrender. The ​Irish law ​of the ​unblemished king ​looks cruel ‌— a ​man maimed ​in his ‌people's victory ​loses his ‌throne — ​but the ‌myth refuses ​both easy ​readings. ​It does ​not mock ​the law: ‌Bres, who ​takes the ‌throne, is ​judged by ‌the same ​standard and ‌falls to ​a blemish ‌of the ​face raised ​by satire. ‌And it ‌does not ‌abandon ​the wounded: ​the whole ‌craft of ​the physician-gods ​bends itself ‌to making ​Nuada whole, ​first in ‌silver, then ​in flesh. ‌What the ​cycle teaches ​is that ​sovereignty is ​not possession ‌but fitness, ‌and fitness ​can ‌be lost ​and restored. ​The silver ‌hand is ‌the emblem ‌of every ‌function that ​has to ‌be rebuilt ​after catastrophe: ​it moves ​in every ‌joint, it ​does the ​work, and ​it is ‌not ​the thing ​it replaces ​— until ‌Miach's deeper ​healing shows ‌that even ​that distinction ‌can be ​overcome. The ‌king who ‌rules again ​is not ​the king ​who fell. ​He is ‌the king ‌who was ​remade.[^1]
